Jeanette Grasselli Brown spent 38 years in industrial research, retiring in 1989 as Director of Corporate Research for BP America, formerly The Standard Oil Company. From 1989 to 1995, she served as Distinguished Visiting Professor and Director of Research Enhancement at Ohio University. In 1995, Governor George Voinovich appointed her to the Ohio Board of Regents, the coordinating body for higher education in the state. She was reappointed by Governor Bob Taft in 1999 and later served as Chair of the Board. In 2002, she was Vice Chair of the Governor’s Commission on Teacher Success.

Brown earned a B.S. from Ohio University and an M.S. in Chemistry from Case Western Reserve University. A noted authority in infrared and Raman spectroscopy, she holds one patent and has authored or co-authored more than 80 publications and nine books. Her areas of expertise include industrial problem solving through vibrational spectroscopy, computerized spectroscopy, process analysis and control, combined instrumental techniques, and environmental spectroscopy. From 1989 to 1995, she served as editor of the international journal Vibrational Spectroscopy. She is a member of Phi Beta Kappa and a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science.

Her professional leadership has extended well beyond the laboratory. Brown has served on the boards of six Fortune 500 corporations, chaired the U.S. National Committee for the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, served as national president of the Society for Applied Spectroscopy, and chaired the Analytical Division of the American Chemical Society. She also served on a White House joint advisory panel evaluating U.S.-Japan science and technology cooperation.

Brown has been deeply involved in Cleveland’s scientific, educational, cultural, and philanthropic institutions. Her civic service has included leadership roles with the Cleveland Hungarian Development Panel, Cleveland Orchestra, Great Lakes Science Center, Cleveland Clinic Foundation, Holden Arboretum, ideastream, Cleveland Scholarship Programs, Northeastern Ohio Science and Engineering Fair, and other organizations. She co-chaired the 2003 Intel International Science and Engineering Fair when it was held in Cleveland.

Her many honors include the American Chemical Society’s Garvan Medal for outstanding achievement by a woman chemist, induction as the first woman in the Ohio Science and Technology Hall of Fame, and membership in the Ohio Women’s Hall of Fame. She has received numerous honorary degrees and distinctions, including the Ellis Island Medal of Honor in 2002 for her work with Cleveland’s Hungarian community, the Great American Award from the Stan Hywet Foundation, and Cleveland State University’s In Tribute to Public Service Award in 2006.

Dr. Dieu Thuc Do was born in Rach Gia, Vietnam, the oldest of five children. His father served as Deputy Chief of Rach Gia, while his mother was a homemaker. He graduated from Saigon Medical School in 1965 and later served in the Army of the Republic of Vietnam (ARVN) as a physician and major. From 1973 to 1975, he was elected chairman of the Rach Gia City Council.

Following the fall of South Vietnam in 1975, Dr. Do immigrated to the United States. After completing the required equivalency examinations and residency training, he was able to resume practicing medicine. He married Thuy Do and settled in Cleveland, Ohio, where they raised three children: Francis, Stephanie, and Jennifer.

Beginning in 1980, Dr. Do practiced medicine in Cleveland and became a respected physician within the community. Known for his empathy and attention to patients’ personal values, cultural backgrounds, and autonomy, he developed relationships that often extended beyond the clinical setting. Many patients regarded him not only as a healthcare provider but also as a trusted member of their families and communities.

At the same time, Dr. Do continued his military service in the United States Army Reserve. In 1991, he served during Operation Desert Storm in Iraq and later retired with the rank of major. He has remained active in local commemorations honoring American and Vietnamese veterans, particularly on Veterans Day and April 30, the anniversary of the fall of Saigon.

Dr. Do’s civic work has been especially important within Cleveland’s Vietnamese and Asian-American communities. He co-founded the Asian Pacific American Federation in Cleveland, served on the Cleveland Mayor’s Advisory Committee from 1983 to 1993, and was president of the Vietnamese Community in Greater Cleveland from 1980 to 1988. During those years, he also acted as a liaison between local government and newly arrived Vietnamese immigrants, helping families navigate life in the United States.

A practicing Catholic, Dr. Do has also been active with the Diocese of Cleveland, the Vietnamese Catholic Community at St. Boniface, and the Diocese’s Asian Ministry. He served on the Board of Trustees of Cleveland Catholic Charities and participated in diocesan vocational efforts.

Dr. Do and his family have long worked to preserve Vietnamese culture while building connections across Cleveland’s diverse communities. They have participated in cultural and civic programs throughout Northeast Ohio, including the Lorain International Festival and the Diocese of Cleveland’s Church in the City initiative. As members of Cleveland’s first generation of Vietnamese immigrants, they have viewed cultural exchange as a way to strengthen the wider community.

Throughout his life, Dr. Do has combined medicine, military service, civic leadership, faith, and cultural advocacy. His career reflects both the experience of rebuilding a life after immigration and a sustained commitment to serving Cleveland’s Vietnamese community and the city as a whole.

Robert “Bob” Haas was born and raised on Cleveland’s West Side. He graduated from St. Edward High School, attended John Carroll University, and later completed training at the Ohio Highway Patrol Police Academy. Haas spent 35 years in public service with the City of Berea Police Department, beginning as a patrol officer, then serving as a detective, and later as the department’s Community Relations Officer until his retirement in 2010.

During his police career, Haas became deeply involved in community safety and neighborhood programs. He founded Berea’s Block Watch program and played an important role in establishing the city’s Safety Town initiative. His work reflected a broader interest in strengthening community ties and creating opportunities for residents to connect with one another.

Haas’s German heritage also became a major part of his civic life. His grandparents immigrated from Germany, and his parents raised him with a strong appreciation for German customs, food, music, and traditions. Some of his fondest childhood memories include family visits to Kiefer’s Restaurant on Detroit Avenue and West 25th Street, as well as holiday celebrations centered on German traditions.

While working as a police officer, Haas became familiar with the Oktoberfest events held at the Cuyahoga County Fairgrounds. After the festival left Berea and eventually faded, he became determined to bring the tradition back. In 2005, with help from volunteers from the Berea Kiwanis, Berea Rotary, and the Donauschwaben community, Haas revived the event as the Cleveland Oktoberfest.

Under his leadership as founder and executive director, the Cleveland Oktoberfest grew into one of the region’s major cultural festivals, celebrating German heritage through music, dance, food, and community traditions. Haas also served on the board of the Cuyahoga County Fairgrounds, helping strengthen the event’s long-term connection to its Berea location.

Recognizing that many other ethnic festivals in Greater Cleveland were struggling with financial pressures and declining attendance, Haas expanded the Oktoberfest’s mission beyond German culture. He founded the William F. Miller International Pavilion, creating a venue where cultural groups from throughout the region could present traditional music, dance, and customs. The pavilion has featured performers representing more than 20 different ethnic communities.

For Haas, the festival became a way to celebrate both cultural distinction and shared experience. He has often emphasized that while communities may differ in language, food, dress, and geography, they are connected by common traditions of celebration, family, music, dance, and friendship.

Through his career in public safety and his leadership of the Cleveland Oktoberfest, Bob Haas has spent decades bringing people together across neighborhoods and cultural communities. His work reflects a sustained commitment to public service, German-American heritage, and Cleveland’s broader multicultural identity.

Helen Karpinski (1899–2002) was born in Cleveland and raised in Reynoldsville, Pennsylvania, in a large Polish-American family. After leaving school following the eighth grade to work in the silk mills, she returned to Cleveland as a teenager in search of work, with her family eventually following.

She married Johnny Karpinski, a noted amateur boxer and Democratic political organizer in Cleveland’s Polish community. After his death, Helen succeeded him as a precinct committeeperson and built a long political career of her own. She served as a ward leader for 15 years, sat on both county and state Democratic executive committees, and was a delegate or alternate to numerous Democratic National Conventions beginning in 1932. From 1980 to 1984, she served on the Democratic National Committee and its Ethnic Committee.

In 1939, Karpinski became the first woman under Cleveland’s current charter to survive a primary election for City Council. Although she lost the general election, her candidacy became an important milestone for women in Cleveland politics. She continued to encourage and support women candidates throughout her life. As president of the Federated Democratic Women of Ohio, she helped recruit Gertrude Donahey for state treasurer and later chaired Donahey’s successful 1970 campaign, which made Donahey the first woman elected to statewide administrative office in Ohio.

Karpinski was equally committed to Cleveland’s Polish-American community. She served as president of the American Polish Women’s Club, held leadership roles in the Polish Women’s Alliance of America, and participated in the Alliance of Poles and the Polish Congress–Ohio Division. She also helped organize the Ladies Auxiliary of the Polish Legion of American Veterans and founded the Ave Maria Senior Citizens Club at St. Casimir Church.

For more than four decades, Karpinski was active in the Cleveland Cultural Gardens Federation. She helped establish and represent the Polish Cultural Garden, led the effort to install a bust of Marie Curie there, and served for many years as Federation treasurer and later as vice president. Her work in the Gardens deepened her commitment to cooperation and mutual understanding among Cleveland’s ethnic communities.

That goal also shaped her broader civic work. Karpinski helped found the Women’s Cosmopolitan Democratic League and served as its president in 1952. Over the course of her life, she received numerous honors for political leadership, community service, and advocacy for women and ethnic communities, including recognition from the Ohio Democratic Party, Polonia Foundation of Ohio, Baptist Ministers Association, and WomenSpace.

By the time of her 100th birthday, Karpinski was widely recognized as a pioneering figure whose influence crossed generations, gender, and ethnicity. Her legacy lies in the intersection of women’s political advancement, Polish-American civic life, and Cleveland’s multicultural institutions.

He joined the paper in 1960 and held a series of leadership positions, including Promotion Director, Assistant to the Publisher, Director of Labor Relations and Personnel, and Vice President and General Manager, before being named Publisher in 1990. Born in Warren, Ohio, Machaskee began his journalism career as a sports and general assignment reporter for the Warren Tribune. He later earned a bachelor’s degree in marketing from Cleveland State University. CSU awarded him an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters in 1995, followed by honorary degrees from the University of Akron and Heidelberg College.

Beyond journalism, Machaskee became one of Greater Cleveland’s most active civic and international leaders. He served in leadership roles with the Cleveland Orchestra, Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland Council on World Affairs, United Way Services, University Circle Inc., Crime Stoppers of Cuyahoga County, and numerous cultural and educational organizations. He chaired the United Way campaign and later became a Lifetime Director of the organization.

Machaskee has also played a prominent role in international and humanitarian affairs. As Chairman of International Orthodox Christian Charities, he traveled extensively to oversee relief efforts in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Young Humanitarian Award from the Urban League of Cleveland, the International Executive of the Year Award from World Trade Center Cleveland, the Golden Door Award from the International Services Center, and the Ellis Island Medal of Honor. Lonnie Davis McCauley was born in Cleveland on September 19, 1947. She attended Lourdes Academy, earned a B.A. in Sociology from Cleveland State University, and later received a Master’s Degree in Library Science from Kent State University in 1999. As part of her graduate studies, she interned at Trinity College in Dublin, Ireland, fulfilling a lifelong dream, and published her thesis, The Irish Directory of Greater Cleveland.

McCauley devoted much of her life to preserving and promoting Irish culture and history in Cleveland. Her involvement in the Irish-American community began in 1981, when she became Public Relations Secretary for the Irish-American Club, East Side. In 1985, she helped found the Padraic Pearse Center and served as its first president, a position she held for seven terms. Under her leadership, the center established Cleveland’s first Irish-American library. She later helped found a second Irish-American library at the West Side Irish-American Club.

At the East Side Club, McCauley created Voices of Ireland, a program of Irish poetry, music, song, dance, recitation, and drama that was presented for seven years. She also helped introduce Irish-language instruction, adult Irish dance, bodhrán lessons, and visiting Irish speakers to the club. Her commitment was deeply personal as well as organizational: she wrote and recited poetry, studied Irish dance, competed with the Irish Adult Dancers, and participated in the Cleveland Feis with her daughter Caitlin. She also served on the founding board of the Irish Music Academy of Cleveland.

McCauley brought the same dedication to documenting Cleveland’s Irish-American history. She became the first Irish-American Archivist at the Western Reserve Historical Society and was a longtime member of the Irish-American Archives Society. She also served on the Irish Famine Memorial Committee and, in September 2000, presided over the dedication of an 11-ton Celtic cross in the Flats honoring those who died or were forced to emigrate during the Great Famine.

One of McCauley’s most significant public honors came in 2001, when she was selected as Grand Marshal of Cleveland’s St. Patrick’s Day Parade, becoming the first woman to hold that role in the parade’s 134-year history.

McCauley saw the preservation of Irish-American memory as a responsibility to future generations. She once said that without active efforts to preserve that history, those who came before would become “historical ghosts.” Through her archival work, cultural programming, community organizing, and scholarship, she helped ensure that Cleveland’s Irish-American traditions would remain visible and accessible.

Lonnie Davis McCauley died on March 18, 2001. Her legacy endures in the institutions, archives, cultural programs, and community traditions she helped build and sustain.

Irene Morrow built a distinguished career in public service while becoming a prominent leader in Cleveland’s Polish-American and broader nationality communities. She and her husband, Edward, raised six children and later welcomed six grandchildren.

Morrow spent 25 years in public service. She served eight years as Deputy Auditor for Cuyahoga County, where she oversaw county payroll operations and helped modernize record keeping through computerization. She then spent 17 years with the City of Cleveland as Personnel Administrator and Secretary of the Civil Service Commission. In that role, she helped administer testing for a municipal workforce of approximately 10,000 employees across more than 800 job classifications and assisted in introducing computerized systems for test administration and grading.

Although she retired from city government in 1989, Morrow remained professionally active. She began a second career in food management and service, working with golf courses, country clubs, and yacht clubs, and later served as an assistant to the president of Elite Realty.

Her civic and cultural work became an equally important part of her public life. In 1975, she was elected Executive Secretary of the Association of Polish Women. She also became active in local political organizations and was recognized by First Lady Barbara Bush as one of 40 outstanding women achievers in Ohio. In 1985, the Polonia Foundation named her Polish Person of the Year.

Morrow is especially associated with the American Nationalities Movement, a Cleveland-based organization created to promote awareness of nations and peoples living under political oppression. She served as its Executive Secretary and Treasurer from 1975 to 1999 and later became its president. Through the organization, she played a major role in Cleveland’s annual observance of Captive Nations Week, an initiative first proclaimed nationally by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in 1959.

Under Morrow’s leadership, the American Nationalities Movement brought together representatives from dozens of ethnic and nationality groups and helped keep attention focused on communities affected by communism, authoritarian rule, and political domination. Although deeply rooted in her own Polish heritage, Morrow became known for supporting the concerns of many different ethnic communities in Cleveland.

Her work was recognized not only by Polish-American organizations, but also by groups including the United Hungarian Societies and the Vietnamese community. Across decades of public service and civic leadership, Irene Morrow became known for connecting Cleveland’s diverse nationality communities and advocating for cultural memory, freedom, and mutual understanding.

August B. Pust was born in Ljubljana, Slovenia, in 1938 and came to the United States in 1957 as a student and visitor. He became a U.S. citizen in 1970. Over the course of more than three decades in public service, Pust built a distinguished career in multicultural affairs, international relations, citizen diplomacy, and the preservation of immigrant heritage.

Before entering government service, Pust worked professionally as an artist, graphic designer, manager, and art director. He later became deeply involved in Cleveland’s ethnic and international communities, serving as Executive Assistant for Ethnic Affairs and International Relations to Cleveland Mayors George Voinovich and Michael White. In recognition of his service, he was named an Honorary Mayor of Cleveland and received a Key to the City.

From 1991 to 2002, Pust served as Director of Multicultural Affairs and International Relations in the Office of the Governor of Ohio. In that role, he coordinated relationships among municipal, regional, state, and international officials and helped develop trade, humanitarian, educational, cultural, and goodwill missions abroad. His work emphasized citizen diplomacy, professional exchanges, university partnerships, and programs designed to strengthen civil society and democratic institutions.

Pust became a leading advocate for people-to-people diplomacy, particularly through programs connecting young professionals, universities, civic leaders, and international organizations. His efforts contributed to the development of models of American citizen diplomacy that promoted greater understanding across cultures and national borders. In 2002, the National Council for International Visitors recognized him as a “Citizen Diplomat.”

His public service also extended to the federal level. Appointed by President George W. Bush, Pust served from 2001 to 2006 on the U.S. Commission for the Preservation of America’s Heritage Abroad. He also testified before the U.S. Congress on international relations and served on numerous boards and organizations concerned with international exchange, immigrant history, and multicultural affairs.

Pust played an important role in Cleveland’s civic and cultural institutions. He was a founding member of the Greater Cleveland Ethnographic Museum and served as its first chairman. He also helped support the effort to bring the 2004 International Children’s Games to Cleveland, an event that attracted thousands of young athletes from dozens of countries and involved extensive participation from the region’s multicultural communities.

Deeply committed to his Slovenian heritage, Pust has been active in numerous Slovenian-American organizations. He was a founding member and board participant in the Slovenian American Heritage Foundation, Slovenian American National Art Guild, and Slovenian Museum and Archives. As an artist and designer, he also created postcards and postage-stamp designs celebrating Slovenian traditions and culture.

Pust’s contributions have been recognized with numerous honors, including the Ellis Island Medal of Honor, the Ohio Distinguished Service Medal, the American Nationalities Movement Freedom Medal, the “Living the Legacy” award honoring the ideals of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., and the Honorary Order of the Freedom Medal from the President of Slovenia. In 1999, he received an honorary doctorate from Valachia University in Romania.

Throughout his career, August Pust has worked to strengthen relationships among Cleveland’s ethnic communities, public institutions, and international partners. His legacy reflects a sustained commitment to multicultural understanding, citizen diplomacy, immigrant history, and the idea that international cooperation can be built through direct relationships between people and communities.

Raised in the Kinsman neighborhood, he attended A.J. Rickoff Elementary School, Alexander Hamilton Junior High School, and John Adams High School before continuing his education at The Ohio State University, where he participated in ROTC. He later attended Marshall School of Law.

While studying law, Sciria worked at Cleveland City Hall and developed an interest in journalism and police reporting. Over the years, writing became an increasingly important part of his life and eventually placed him at the center of Northeast Ohio’s Italian-American media and cultural community.

In 1992, Sciria acquired La Gazzetta Italiana, becoming the publication’s principal writer and editor as well as handling advertising and subscriptions. Sciria’s commitment to his heritage extended beyond publishing. Proud of both his American identity and his Sicilian heritage, Sciria frequently emphasized the contributions Italians and Italian Americans have made to art, music, literature, industry, science, banking, public service, and American civic life. Paramjit Singh became a prominent leader in Cleveland’s Asian Indian community soon after arriving in the city in June 1962. A Sikh committed to service, he has spent decades building organizations, promoting Indian culture, and strengthening ties between Cleveland’s immigrant communities and the wider civic community.

Singh earned a degree in Mechanical Engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur in 1958 and entered the MBA program at Case Western Reserve University in 1962. He quickly became active in the university’s International Student Group and was soon elected its chairman. That experience brought him into contact with students from around the world and deepened his commitment to intercultural understanding.

As one of Cleveland’s early Indian community leaders, Singh helped introduce local audiences to Indian culture, food, religion, and traditions, including Sikhism. The Cleveland Council on World Affairs invited him to organize an Indian dinner celebrating the 13th Republic Day of India, bringing together students, community members, and international visitors. In 1964, he joined other local leaders in establishing the India Association of Cleveland.

Singh also made a visible statement about cultural identity in 1965 when he became the first turbaned Sikh to participate in a Case Western Reserve University graduation ceremony while wearing his turban rather than the traditional mortarboard.

As immigration reform contributed to the growth of Indian-American communities across the United States, Singh became increasingly involved in regional and national organizations. The National Federation of Indian-American Associations was established in 1980, followed in 1981 by the Federation of India Community Associations of Northeast Ohio, known as FICA. Singh went on to serve as president of FICA and as vice president of NFIA.

Together with his wife, Linda, Singh also helped develop Project SEVA, based on the idea that Indian Americans should give back to the communities that had welcomed them. Working with FICA, Ohio State Senator Michael White, and Rev. Earl Preston Jr. of Morning Star Baptist Church, the initiative organized a Thanksgiving dinner serving approximately 400 people. Singh later brought the idea to NFIA, which adopted Project SEVA as a national service program.

His civic involvement extended across business, engineering, government, and community affairs. Singh served as president of the Cleveland chapter of the American Society of Engineers of Indian Origin, was a founding member of the Asian-Indian-American Business Group and Asian-Indian-Americans for Better Government, and served as an executive member of Cleveland Mayor George Voinovich’s Asian Advisory Council.

Through decades of volunteer service, Paramjit Singh helped shape the institutional foundations of Cleveland’s Indian-American community while promoting cultural understanding, civic participation, and service to others. His work helped connect local Indian organizations with the broader civic life of Cleveland and Northeast Ohio.

George V. Voinovich built a public-service career spanning more than four decades at the local, county, state, and federal levels. He served in the Ohio House of Representatives, as Cuyahoga County Auditor and County Commissioner, as Lieutenant Governor of Ohio, Mayor of Cleveland, Governor of Ohio, and finally as a United States Senator from 1999 to 2011.

Voinovich became Mayor of Cleveland in 1979 at a particularly difficult moment in the city’s history. Cleveland had entered financial default the previous year, and his administration focused on restoring fiscal stability, reorganizing city government, and rebuilding cooperation between City Hall and the business community. His administration created an Operations Improvement Task Force composed of private-sector executives, reorganized city departments, strengthened accounting and auditing systems, and negotiated a debt-repayment agreement that helped move Cleveland out of default. During his tenure, Cleveland received All-America City honors in 1982, 1984, and 1986.

Voinovich also promoted neighborhood redevelopment and major civic projects, including improvements along Cleveland’s lakefront and early development efforts associated with North Coast Harbor, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and the Great Lakes Science Center. His approach emphasized public-private cooperation as a tool for rebuilding the city’s finances, infrastructure, and civic confidence.

After leaving City Hall, Voinovich was elected Governor of Ohio in 1990 and reelected in 1994. He subsequently represented Ohio in the U.S. Senate from 1999 through 2010. In Washington, his work included government management, fiscal policy, environmental issues, and foreign affairs. He served for five years on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and was particularly active on issues involving the Balkans and the emerging democracies of Central and Eastern Europe.

Voinovich was also an advocate of NATO enlargement. At the 2002 NATO Summit in Prague, he joined President George W. Bush as invitations to membership were extended to Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. His international work also addressed U.S. public diplomacy, Southeast European stability, United Nations reform, and efforts against antisemitism, racism, and other forms of intolerance.

Born and raised in Cleveland, Voinovich maintained particularly strong ties to the city’s ethnic communities. His father was of Serbian heritage and his mother was Slovenian-American, and Voinovich frequently spoke about ethnic heritage as an important part of American civic identity. His family’s roots were especially deep in Cleveland’s Collinwood and Slovenian communities.

Throughout his career, Voinovich emphasized public service, fiscal responsibility, cooperation across institutions, and stronger connections between government and the communities it served. He remained closely identified with Cleveland throughout his life and continued living in his longtime Collinwood home after leaving public office.

George V. Voinovich died on June 12, 2016, at age 79. He and his wife, Janet, were married for 54 years and raised four children. His career left a lasting mark on Cleveland, the State of Ohio, and the nation, particularly through his role in guiding Cleveland out of financial default and his later work in state government and international affairs.

Leo Weidenthal (1878–1967) was a Cleveland journalist, civic leader, and founder of what became the Cleveland Cultural Gardens Federation. Born in Cleveland to Emanuel and Julia Kretch Weidenthal, he spent much of his life promoting journalism, intercultural understanding, literature, and the civic life of his hometown.

Weidenthal began his newspaper career as a reporter for the Cleveland World and later worked for the Cleveland Leader. In 1906, he joined The Plain Dealer, where he covered City Hall. Known for his persistence as a reporter, he earned the nickname “Leo the Lion of Willowdale.” When he left daily newspaper reporting in 1917, Cleveland City Council unanimously voted to name a street in his honor—Willowdale Avenue, a loose English translation of the name Weidenthal.

In 1917, Weidenthal became editor of the Jewish Independent, a weekly newspaper founded by his brother Maurice in 1906. He guided the publication for 47 years, remaining one of the most influential voices in Cleveland’s Jewish press until his retirement in 1964. His retirement helped prompt the reorganization of the city’s Jewish press under the Cleveland Jewish Publication Company.

Weidenthal also played an important role in Cleveland’s interfaith and intercultural life. He was a founder of the Cleveland chapter of the National Conference of Christians and Jews, helping make Cleveland one of the first American cities to establish a chapter of the organization.

His most enduring civic legacy, however, grew from his passion for William Shakespeare. Weidenthal assembled and catalogued an extensive Shakespeare collection that later became part of the Cleveland Public Library. In 1916, marking the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death, he persuaded Cleveland leaders to establish a Shakespeare Garden in Rockefeller Park.

At the dedication of the Shakespeare Garden, Weidenthal proposed an even broader idea: that similar gardens should be created to represent each of Cleveland’s nationality communities. That vision gradually developed into the Cleveland Cultural Gardens. By 1926, the Cultural Garden League had been organized, and in 1927 the City of Cleveland formally reserved sections of Rockefeller Park for the development of future nationality gardens.

Through the Cultural Gardens, Weidenthal envisioned Cleveland’s many immigrant and ethnic communities represented side by side in a shared public landscape. The project became one of the city’s most distinctive expressions of multicultural identity and international fellowship.

Weidenthal remained closely associated with Cleveland civic life throughout his career. In 1962, Cleveland Press editor Louis B. Seltzer praised him as one of the citizens who had done the most in his generation to sustain the greatness of the city.

Through journalism, cultural preservation, interfaith work, and the creation of the Cleveland Cultural Gardens movement, Leo Weidenthal left a lasting mark on Cleveland’s civic and cultural landscape.

Vijaya Lakshmi Emani was born in Kurnool, India, to Indurani and G. Venkataramana Reddy. Known for her determination, energy, and high standards, she excelled academically from an early age. She graduated from Osmania University in 1980 with a B.S. in Electronics and Communications Engineering and immigrated to the United States in 1986. She later earned an M.S. in Computer Science from Cleveland State University.

Emani built a life in Cleveland while raising her two daughters, Sujata and Nirmala, with the support of her mother. Her experiences as an immigrant and single parent shaped much of her later civic work, particularly her advocacy for women, families, and newcomers navigating difficult transitions.

She first became active in Northeast Ohio’s Indian community through the Northeast Ohio Telugu Association and later through the Federation of India Community Associations, or FICA. She eventually served as president of FICA and became a prominent voice in Cleveland’s broader Asian-American community.

Emani used her leadership positions to address issues that were often left unspoken. She helped create support networks for single parents and encouraged public discussion of domestic violence within immigrant communities. Her work combined cultural advocacy with practical efforts to make community institutions more responsive to women and families facing hardship.

She also played an important role in the development of the India Cultural Garden in Cleveland. Beginning in the early 2000s, Emani worked to build support for the project, contributing to the 2005 groundbreaking and the installation of a statue of Mahatma Gandhi in 2006. Her involvement helped establish a permanent representation of Indian heritage within the Cleveland Cultural Gardens.

Beyond these efforts, Emani was active in a wide range of civic and cultural organizations and became known as an advocate for community participation, cultural understanding, and women’s empowerment. Her leadership style reflected a belief she often expressed: “You can have excellence, you can have excuses, but you cannot have both.”

Emani died tragically in 2009 after being struck by a tractor-trailer while standing near her disabled vehicle on the Ohio Turnpike in Portage County. Her death was deeply felt across Cleveland’s Indian and Asian-American communities.

Her legacy endures through the organizations she strengthened, the cultural institutions she helped build, and the people she encouraged to participate more fully in civic life. Vijaya Lakshmi Emani is remembered as a community leader, advocate, educator, caregiver, and champion for women and immigrant families.

Luis Martinez was born in Bayamón, Puerto Rico, and moved with his family to Lorain, Ohio, when he was three years old. He graduated from Lorain Admiral King High School in 1966 and later served with the U.S. Marine Corps in Vietnam. During his service with a Combined Action Group, he was wounded in combat and received two Purple Hearts.

Martinez later contributed the chapter “A Puerto Rican Marine” to Everything We Had: An Oral History of the Vietnam War by Thirty-Three American Soldiers Who Fought It, edited by Al Santoli and published by Random House in 1981. His testimony helped document the experiences of Puerto Rican and Latino servicemen during the Vietnam War.

In 1973, Martinez moved to Cleveland and joined the Recruitment and Training Program/Construction Equal Employment Plan, known as RTP/CEEP. The program helped minority youth and women prepare for aptitude tests and gain access to building and construction trade union apprenticeship programs. Martinez was eventually promoted to Project Director. During this period, he attended Harvard University’s John F. Kennedy School of Government, where he earned a certificate in Manpower Administration.

In 1981, Martinez briefly served with the U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of Apprenticeship and Training before being appointed by Cleveland Mayor George V. Voinovich as an Executive Assistant and liaison between the Mayor’s Office and Cleveland’s Hispanic community.

During six years in that role, Martinez worked with public and private organizations to expand opportunities for Latino residents and strengthen communication with City Hall. He collaborated in the creation and development of organizations including Esperanza, Inc., then known as the Cleveland Hispanic Scholarship Fund. He also advocated for greater Latino representation within the Cleveland Police Department, Fire Department, and other city agencies, while supporting Hispanic-owned businesses seeking municipal contracts.

In 1986, Martinez received a scholarship from the National Urban Fellows program and earned a Master of Public Administration from Baruch College of the City University of New York. After returning to Cleveland, he joined the City of Cleveland Department of Community Development, where he served in several project leadership roles until his retirement in 2010.

Throughout his career, Martinez combined public service with advocacy for Cleveland’s Puerto Rican and Latino communities. His work focused on employment access, education, economic opportunity, representation in city government, and stronger connections between Hispanic residents and public institutions.

Martinez is married to Nora Martinez, a retired Cleveland Municipal School District teacher. Together they raised two children, Luis Carlos and Lynna M. Martinez, both of whom pursued careers in education and student development.

The Reverend Dr. Otis Moss, Jr. is a theologian, pastor, civil rights advocate, and civic leader whose career has connected the Black church, social justice, education, and public service.

Born in LaGrange, Georgia, Moss earned his bachelor’s degree from Morehouse College, a Master of Divinity from the Morehouse School of Religion at the Interdenominational Theological Center, and a Doctor of Ministry from United Theological Seminary.

Before coming to Cleveland, Moss served churches in Georgia and Ohio, including Mount Olive Baptist Church in LaGrange, Providence Baptist Church in Atlanta, Mount Zion Baptist Church in Lockland, Ohio, and Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, where he served as co-pastor with the Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. He was also active in the Southern Christian Leadership Conference during the leadership of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., serving as a board member and regional director.

Moss became pastor of Olivet Institutional Baptist Church in Cleveland and led the congregation for 33 years before retiring in 2008. Under his leadership, Olivet became an important center of religious, civic, and social life in Cleveland. His ministry consistently emphasized education, civil and human rights, economic justice, health, and community responsibility.

In 1997, Moss helped establish the Otis Moss, Jr.–University Hospitals Health Center through a partnership between Olivet Institutional Baptist Church and University Hospitals. Moss served on the boards of organizations including the Cleveland Museum of Art and the Cleveland Foundation and spent more than a decade as chairman of the Morehouse College Board of Trustees. He was also a national board member and trustee of the Martin Luther King, Jr. Center for Nonviolent Social Change.

He served as an adviser to President Jimmy Carter during discussions at Camp David and attended the 1994 signing of the Israel-Jordan peace treaty as a guest of President Bill Clinton. He later served on President Barack Obama’s White House Council on Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships. In 2009, he toured India with Rajmohan Gandhi, grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, lecturing on the legacies of Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

In Cleveland, his legacy is especially visible through Olivet Institutional Baptist Church, his work in civil rights and community health, and his role as a mentor and civic leader across generations.

Moss is married to Edwina Hudson Moss and is the father of Kevin Moss, the late Daphne Moss, and the Rev. Otis Moss III.

Ralph J. Perk (1914–1999) was a Cleveland political and civic leader who served as the city’s mayor from 1971 to 1977. Born and raised in Cleveland, he spent much of his life in the Broadway-Fleet neighborhood and built his political career around municipal service, ethnic-community involvement, regional government, and opposition to communist and totalitarian rule.

Perk entered local politics through the 13th Ward Republican organization and was elected to Cleveland City Council in 1953, representing the Broadway–East 55th Street area for five terms. In 1962, he was elected Cuyahoga County Auditor and subsequently won two additional terms. He was elected mayor in 1971, succeeding Carl Stokes, and was reelected in 1973 and 1975 before losing his bid for another term in 1977.

As mayor, Perk promoted the regionalization of major public services. His administration helped establish the Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District and played an important role in the negotiations that created the Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Authority in 1975. His administration also expanded emergency medical services, pursued improvements at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport, and oversaw a number of downtown development and public-building projects.

Perk maintained relationships with national Republican leaders and used Cleveland’s position as a major urban center to seek federal assistance for city programs. During a period of significant fiscal pressure, his administration obtained federal revenue-sharing and grant funds for public safety and other municipal needs. He also promoted regional cooperation as a way to address problems that extended beyond Cleveland’s city limits.

A central part of Perk’s civic life was his involvement with Cleveland’s immigrant and nationality communities. In 1959, he founded and chaired the American Nationalities Movement of Greater Cleveland, an umbrella organization representing dozens of nationality groups. The organization became closely associated with Cleveland observances of Captive Nations Week, the national commemoration established by Congress and proclaimed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in 1959 to draw attention to peoples living under communist domination.

Perk viewed Cleveland’s ethnic and cultural diversity as an important civic asset and worked to give nationality communities a greater presence in municipal affairs. His administration included staff and programs concerned specifically with nationality and international affairs, while his broader civic work encouraged cooperation among Cleveland’s Polish, Slovenian, Ukrainian, Hungarian, Baltic, and other immigrant communities.

A lifelong Roman Catholic, Perk lived with his wife, Lucille, and their seven children in the Broadway-Fleet neighborhood. Even after leaving elected office, he remained involved in civic affairs and continued his work with the American Nationalities Movement. He died in 1999.

Ralph Perk’s legacy in Cleveland is closely associated with regional public services, municipal government, and the city’s nationality communities, particularly his efforts to bring ethnic and international concerns into Cleveland civic life.

Tony Petkovsek became one of Cleveland’s best-known ambassadors of Slovenian culture and Cleveland-style polka music through a broadcasting career that began in 1961. For decades, he produced and hosted a daily radio program combining polka music with interviews, community news, travel information, and conversations with civic and entertainment figures. His program aired on WELW 1330 AM and, earlier in his career, on stations including WXEN, WZAK, WBOE, and WCPN.

Much of Petkovsek’s broadcasting was closely tied to Cleveland’s Slovenian community. For many years, programs originated from Tony’s Polka Village and the Polka Tour Headquarters of Kollander World Travel on East 185th Street. He later broadcast from his own studio in Fairport Harbor. Through radio, live events, travel, and community organizing, he became widely known as Cleveland’s “Polka Ambassador.”

Petkovsek also played an important role in developing polka tourism. As vice president and co-owner of Kollander Travel, he organized his first polka music tour in 1967 and went on to arrange and host trips for thousands of travelers throughout the United States and internationally. His tours helped introduce Cleveland-style polka and Slovenian-American culture to audiences around the world.

His radio work developed into a broader network of community service. Petkovsek established the Cleveland Slovenian Radio Club, whose volunteers organized fundraising campaigns and cultural events. Through radiothons and other activities, the group raised funds for causes including the Slovene Home for the Aged and, in the early 1990s, efforts supporting international recognition of newly independent Slovenia.

The Radio Club also sponsored annual Thanksgiving festivals that became major gatherings for Slovenian-American and polka communities. Held over the years at venues including the Slovenian National Home on St. Clair Avenue, St. Joseph High School on East 185th Street, and downtown Cleveland hotels, the festivals attracted visitors from across the United States, Canada, and Europe.

In 1987, Petkovsek called the meeting that led to the creation of the American Slovenian Polka Foundation, sponsor of the National Cleveland-Style Polka Hall of Fame and Museum. He became its founding chairman and was himself inducted as a Lifetime Achiever in 1992. The organization helped preserve the history, music, recordings, and personalities associated with the distinctive Cleveland style of polka.

Petkovsek was also active in neighborhood and civic affairs. He helped organize major outdoor festivals along East 185th Street and served on the board of the Northeast Shores Development Corporation. Former Cleveland mayors George Voinovich and Michael White appointed him to the city’s Board of Zoning Appeals. He later served on the Ohio Arts Council under Governor Voinovich and acted as master of ceremonies for two of Voinovich’s gubernatorial inaugurations.

Over the course of his career, Petkovsek received numerous awards, proclamations, and honors for broadcasting, cultural preservation, and community service. In 1967, at age 25, he was named Slovenian Man of the Year by the Federation of Slovenian Homes, and in 1991 he was inducted into the National Broadcasters Hall of Fame.

Through radio, travel, festivals, civic service, and the preservation of Cleveland-style polka, Tony Petkovsek helped make Slovenian-American culture a visible and enduring part of Cleveland’s identity.

Gerald M. “Gerry” Quinn was an award-winning broadcaster and community leader who played a major role in preserving and promoting Irish culture in Greater Cleveland. Born in Garracloon, County Mayo, Ireland, a small rural community near Ballina, Quinn later settled in Euclid, Ohio, where he became one of the region’s most recognizable voices in Irish-American civic and cultural life.

Quinn attended the local National School near Ballina, where his father, Liam Quinn, served as schoolmaster. After coming to the United States, he made Cleveland his home and married Nellie Stack, whose family also had deep Irish roots. Together they raised six children.

Professionally, Quinn worked as a project manager in construction and engineering. In 1979, while managing construction of a pharmaceutical plant in Dublin, he had a long telephone conversation about Ireland with his friend Leo D’Arcy, who managed a radio station in Willoughby. The conversation was recorded and led directly to Quinn being offered his own radio program.

That opportunity launched a broadcasting career that lasted more than three decades. His weekly program, Gerry Quinn Irish Radio, aired on WHK 1420 and became an important connection between Cleveland-area Irish Americans and the music, news, traditions, and culture of Ireland. The program received an Achievement in Radio Award and was recognized as one of Northeast Ohio’s leading ethnic radio programs.

Quinn’s contribution extended far beyond broadcasting. In 1978, he conceived and chaired the effort that led to the founding of the Irish American Club – East Side, helping create a permanent cultural and social home for Irish Americans in the region. Decades later, in 2004, he also helped establish the Mayo Society, strengthening connections among Clevelanders with roots in County Mayo.

Through these organizations and his radio work, Quinn helped preserve Irish heritage while creating opportunities for younger generations to remain connected to the history, music, and traditions of Ireland.

In recognition of his decades of cultural and community leadership, Quinn was selected as Grand Marshal of Cleveland’s St. Patrick’s Day Parade in 2011.

Through broadcasting, institution-building, and community organizing, Gerry Quinn became a central figure in Cleveland’s Irish-American community and helped ensure that Irish cultural life remained visible and vibrant across Northeast Ohio.

Albert B. Ratner was a Cleveland business leader, real estate developer, philanthropist, and civic advocate whose career was closely tied to the transformation of downtown Cleveland and the growth of the city’s Jewish community.

Ratner spent much of his professional life with Forest City Enterprises, joining the family business in 1951 and eventually becoming co-chairman of its board. Over the course of his career, he helped guide the company’s expansion in commercial and residential real estate and became one of the most influential figures in Cleveland development.

His most visible impact on the city came through Forest City’s redevelopment of the Terminal Tower and former Union Terminal into Tower City Center. Completed in 1990, the project combined retail, office, hotel, and transit functions in the heart of downtown Cleveland. It became one of the signature redevelopment projects of the era and helped spur renewed investment in the city center during the 1990s.

Ratner was also deeply involved in Cleveland civic life. He served with organizations including the Greater Cleveland Partnership, United Way, Cleveland Initiative for Education, Shoes and Clothes for Kids, and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Foundation. His leadership consistently connected business development with broader civic and philanthropic goals.

Within Cleveland’s Jewish community, Ratner held especially important leadership roles. He was a life trustee of the Jewish Community Federation of Cleveland and served on national and international Jewish organizations, including the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee and United Jewish Communities. His work reflected a long-standing commitment to philanthropy, Jewish communal life, and international humanitarian causes.

Ratner also served on corporate and nonprofit boards beyond Cleveland, including American Greetings, RPM, Inc., the Henry M. Jackson Foundation, and the Enterprise Foundation. His influence extended into education as well, including service as an adjunct visiting professor with Michigan State University’s Land Policy Institute.

A graduate of Michigan State University with a degree in forestry, Ratner later received honorary degrees from Long Island University and Polytechnic University.

Through Forest City Enterprises, philanthropy, Jewish communal leadership, and civic service, Albert Ratner played a major role in shaping modern Cleveland. His legacy is especially visible in downtown redevelopment, community institutions, and the long-term effort to strengthen Cleveland as a place to live, work, and invest.

Luong Thi Gia Hoa Ryan was born in Vietnam, the oldest of twelve children. During the Vietnam War, she worked for the U.S. government as an interpreter and secretary and supervised local employees. She immigrated to the United States in 1971 and went on to build a career spanning business, public service, refugee assistance, and community advocacy.

Ryan became an entrepreneur in Northeast Ohio, opening and operating the Moonlight Restaurant in Lorain as well as other food-service businesses. She later became manager and director of Sai Gon Plaza, which developed into an important cultural and community gathering place for Vietnamese and Asian residents.

Her public-service career has included extensive work with the City of Cleveland. Appointed by Cleveland City Council, she served on the city’s Community Relations Board under three mayors. She also served on the board of the Lorain County Alcoholism and Drug Abuse Services organization and worked with numerous community groups addressing health, education, social services, and immigrant needs.

Beginning in 1975, Ryan became deeply involved in the resettlement of Vietnamese and other Indochinese refugees and immigrants. She helped newcomers navigate life in the United States while advocating for access to social services, healthcare, education, and cultural support.

In the early 1980s, Ryan founded an Asian Women’s Support Group and became active in the Lorain International Festival. In 1995, she helped host the festival when Vietnam and the Vietnamese community were featured. She has also worked closely with American and Vietnamese veterans’ organizations and has lectured and taught on Asian food, culture, and society.

Ryan is the founder and executive director of the Friendship Foundation of American-Vietnamese. Through the organization, she helped organize more than 20 humanitarian missions to Vietnam, involving over 1,000 volunteers and providing millions of dollars in medical supplies, equipment, educational materials, services, and other assistance.

She also developed the original concept for the Asian Community Project, later incorporated into Bridgeway, and served as its coordinator from 1997 to 2003. The program provided mental health services to Vietnamese, Laotian, Cambodian, and other Asian families, as well as citizenship and English-language classes for older adults and seniors.

Ryan has also worked to strengthen international relationships between Cleveland and Vietnam. She hosted Vietnamese delegations visiting Cleveland for business, educational, and cultural exchanges, participated in an international law conference in Vietnam, and in 2008 hosted a delegation of 15 Vietnamese lawyers for an extended professional visit to the United States and Northeast Ohio.

Through decades of civic service, humanitarian work, cultural advocacy, and immigrant assistance, Gia Hoa Ryan has played an important role in connecting Cleveland’s Asian and Vietnamese communities with local government, social services, and international partners.

Lucretia Stoica was a longtime Cleveland civic leader, immigrant advocate, and international-relations professional whose career focused on helping newcomers build lives in the United States and strengthening understanding among the region’s many ethnic communities.

Born in Youngstown, Ohio, Stoica spent much of her childhood and young adulthood in Romania, where she completed university studies in law, literature, and philosophy. Following World War II, she was among the Americans repatriated from Europe by the U.S. government and returned to Ohio.

After settling in Cleveland, Stoica joined the International Institute of the YWCA, an immigrant-service organization later known as the International Services Center. She began as a caseworker, became deputy director, and ultimately served as executive director for 26 years. When she retired in 1988, she had completed 41 years of service with the organization.

Throughout her career, Stoica became a leading advocate for immigrants and refugees in Northeast Ohio. Her work ranged from individual case assistance to immigration policy and public education. She defended immigrants in immigration and deportation proceedings, volunteered as an instructor for an Immigration and Naturalization Service outreach program, and spent three decades publishing a news bulletin that informed immigrants, refugees, and community organizations about changes in federal laws and regulations. She also testified before Congress and at public hearings on legislation affecting immigrant and refugee communities.

Beginning in the 1950s, Stoica organized conferences and cultural festivals highlighting the histories and contributions of Cleveland’s nationality communities. These programs became models for other organizations seeking to promote intercultural understanding.

In the late 1960s, with support from the Ford Foundation, Stoica founded and directed Project Bridge, an initiative designed to improve understanding and cooperation among Cleveland’s nationality, racial, and ethnic communities. For six years, she simultaneously led Project Bridge and the Nationalities Services Center.

Stoica was also one of four women who co-founded the Language Bank of Cleveland in the early 1970s. The program provided free translation and interpretation services to hospitals, schools, courts, visitor organizations, and other public and private institutions, making essential services more accessible to residents with limited English proficiency.

Another major part of her work involved documenting Cleveland and Ohio’s ethnic organizations. For approximately four decades, she edited and published the Nationality Directory, originally created by journalist Theodore Andrica. The directory documented thousands of ethnic organizations across Ohio, recording their leadership, addresses, and histories and preserving an important record of the state’s immigrant communities.

Stoica also played a central role in refugee resettlement. She founded the Cleveland Refugee Resettlement Committee and served for several years as chair of the Ohio Refugee Advisory Council, working on policies and programs affecting newly arrived refugees.

Her civic involvement extended across numerous Cleveland and Ohio institutions, including the Ohio Arts Council, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland International Programs, Cleveland Bicentennial Commission, Playhouse Square Foundation, Cleveland Commission on Aging, United Nations-related organizations, and cultural heritage initiatives.

Through four decades of leadership, Lucretia Stoica helped build much of the institutional infrastructure that supported immigrants and refugees in Cleveland. Her work in resettlement, language access, cultural preservation, and interethnic cooperation made her an important figure in the development of Cleveland’s multicultural civic community.
